question.text:
You are analyzing the performance of two technology stocks over the past year: Stock A: Return = 15%, Beta = 1.2 Stock B: Return = 12%, Beta = 0.9
Calculate the Treynor Ratio for Stock A assuming a risk-free rate of 2%.

explanation.text: The Logic: Per the workbook, Treynor Ratio = (Return − Risk-Free Rate) / Beta, using beta as the denominator (in contrast with Sharpe, which uses standard deviation). For Stock A: (15% − 2%) / 1.2 = 10.83%. The Trap: 8.33% tempts those who divide by the wrong denominator. 12.33% tempts candidates who forget to subtract the risk-free rate. 14.83% tempts those who use the wrong beta value. The conceptual trap is confusing Treynor (denominator = beta) with Sharpe (denominator = standard deviation). Note: Because the stem provides beta but not standard deviation, the Sharpe ratio cannot be computed here; Treynor is the appropriate measure.
